An Afghani mujahideen soldier aims an American supplied Stinger missile at passing Soviet aircraft near a remote rebel base in the Safed Koh Mountains. 1988.

The FIM-92 Stinger is an infrared homing surface-to-air missile (SAM).

In late 1985, several American groups began arguing the CIA was not doing enough to support the Mujahideen in the Soviet–Afghan War. The idea was controversial because up to that point, the CIA had been operating with the pretense that the US was not involved in the war directly. All weapons supplied at that point were non-U.S. made weapons, like Type 56 rifles purchased from China, and AK-47 derivatives purchased from Egypt.

The CIA eventually supplied nearly 500 Stingers (some sources claim 1,500–2,000) to the Mujahideen in Afghanistan with the supply of 250 launchers. According to a 1993 US Air Defense Artillery publication, the Mujahideen gunners used the Stingers to score approximately 269 total aircraft kills in about 340 engagements, a 79-percent kill ratio.

After the 1989 Soviet withdrawal from Afghanistan, the U.S. attempted to buy back around 300 missiles for US$183,300 each. The U.S. collected many of the Stingers it had delivered, but by 1996 around 600 were unaccounted for and some found their way into Croatia, Iran, Sri Lanka, Qatar and North Korea.
